author: Claude (EFL materials writer role), v2 against the quality gate
basis: placeholder Claude revised slides 3, 9, 10, 11 against the v2 gate.

slides.1: Gender equality is usually described as a women's issue, although the fifth global goal is really about the ambitions a society is prepared to restrict. Today I want to examine what genuine equality would demand from everybody here.
slides.2: Why should the men here care? Because the evidence links women's progress to stronger households, better schools and faster economic growth, which means that excluding half a population is an expensive habit rather than a neutral tradition.
slides.3: Picture a bird trying to fly with one wing deliberately held down. Societies repeat that experiment whenever they restrict half their members, and the altitude lost is paid for by everybody on board, not only by women.
slides.4: Historically a boy was expected to enter medicine while his sister stayed at home. Those assumptions still operate as invisible walls, steering teenagers away from the subjects they would otherwise have chosen.
slides.5: The conditioning starts long before anybody mentions careers, because shops still divide their shelves into vehicles for sons and dolls for daughters. Children read that message quickly, learning to imagine only one category of future.
slides.6: Globally, poverty pulls girls out of the classroom long before graduation, leaving many families to educate only the son. Denied literacy, a daughter tends to earn less throughout her life, so the disadvantage is inherited rather than solved.
slides.7: Turn to pay. Women still earn less than men on average, and a measurable gap survives even after economists control for occupation, hours and experience, which suggests the problem is structural rather than personal.
slides.8: Climb any large organisation and the share of women falls sharply near the top, a barrier commonly called the glass ceiling. Positions held by one half of the population produce decisions shaped by one half of the evidence.
slides.9: Unpaid domestic labour is the least visible inequality of all, since cleaning, cooking and childcare still fall primarily to women. Only when families redistribute that load will those hours return for study, promotion and rest.
slides.10: Real change originates in language, because the way we speak inside a classroom quietly determines what feels normal. Listening properly, refusing to judge anybody by gender and never allocating a job by sex cost nothing.
slides.11: Equality at home is demonstrated rather than announced, so encourage sons to cook a decent meal and daughters to repair a bicycle. Families who genuinely share the work tend to argue about it considerably less.
slides.12: Allyship costs something, which is precisely why it matters. What keeps a bully going is silence, not agreement, so one audible objection in a lecture hall can change the atmosphere of a whole year group.
slides.13: The encouraging news is that girls are entering robotics teams, coding clubs and space projects in far larger numbers. Recruiting from the whole population rather than half of it produces better engineering, and nobody has answered that argument yet.
slides.14: Connectivity has quietly rewritten who can study. A girl in an isolated village can follow an entire course on a borrowed tablet, which means geography no longer decides how far an education can travel.
slides.15: Social media now broadcasts careers that earlier generations never saw. Stories written by athletes, artists and leaders reach a teenager scrolling at midnight, arguing quietly that her own future could contain rather more than she assumed.
slides.16: Legislation is moving as well. Several governments now require equal pay and safer workplaces, partly because economists keep reporting that full participation tends to raise national output rather than merely redistribute it.
slides.17: So where does the argument stand? We have traced inherited attitudes, unequal pay and unpaid work, and set against them new laws, technology and role models, which together make equality a programme rather than a wish.
slides.18: My own commitment is small but specific. I will treat every classmate as an equal and say something when somebody does not, and I would ask each of you to choose one comparable action before tonight.
slides.19: Structural change is slow, and pretending otherwise would insult everyone already working at it. The agenda names 2030, so the honest question is not whether we arrive on time but how much closer our generation can pull that date.
slides.20: SDG 5 is not a request addressed to somebody else. When women and men participate as equals, households, companies and whole economies tend to do better, and I have already chosen my side.
